canonical_term: Nine Princes in Amber (1970) Chapter 1 witness
definition: The selected first-edition opening-chapter witness: Roger Zelazny’s Nine Princes in Amber, published by Doubleday in 1970.
cultural_caution: This is a specific printed-edition and chapter boundary, not a merge of later novels, posthumous or other-author continuations, adaptations, games, translations, or reader reference summaries.

citations.locator: Nine princes in amber; Roger Zelazny; [1st ed.], Doubleday, Garden City, N.Y., 1970

definition: The named hospital setting of the selected opening chapter.
cultural_caution: A fictional place/institution term, not a character node and not evidence about real hospitals, psychiatric care, medication, disability, coercion, or professional practice.

citations.locator: Roger Zelazny, Nine princes in amber, [1st ed.], Doubleday, 1970; Chapter 1
supports: Greenwood as the opening hospital setting

definition: The opening narrative condition in which the narrator reports missing personal memories and seeks information about his situation.
cultural_caution: The creator discusses amnesia as a narrative device. This term does not diagnose the character, establish a medical cause or treatment, generalize about disability or mental health, or imply unreliable testimony in every respect.

citations.locator: ‘Some Sort of Family Squabble,’ Roger Zelazny retrospective interview excerpt
supports: amnesia as the opening information-discovery device

citations.locator: Roger Zelazny, Nine princes in amber, [1st ed.], Doubleday, 1970; Chapter 1
supports: the chapter-level primary witness for the narrator’s reported memory gap

definition: The selected chapter’s limited first-person structure: the narrator and reader receive incomplete information about his identity and circumstances.
cultural_caution: A formal narrative description, not a clinical, legal, moral, or philosophical claim about personal identity. It does not license importing later revelations or treating the character’s local name as permanently settled.

citations.locator: ‘Some Sort of Family Squabble,’ Roger Zelazny retrospective interview excerpt
supports: Zelazny’s explanation that the protagonist learns answers alongside the reader because of memory loss
